titre: Future in the past (was going to, would)
intro: “I was going to call you, but I forgot”, “I knew he would come”, “We were about to leave”: to talk about the future as seen from a moment in the past, English uses was going to, would, was about to, was + -ing and was to. You need these forms to tell stories, apologise for plans that didn't happen and report what people said.
objectifs: Express a past intention or prediction with was / were going to, often one that did not happen.
Use would for the future seen from the past in stories and reported speech.
Use was about to, was + -ing, was due to and was to according to the meaning.
Avoid “would” after when / as soon as.

sections.titre: The principle: move the point of view into the past
texte: Each way of talking about the future has a “past” equivalent: you simply move the auxiliary back. will → would; am going to → was going to; am meeting → was meeting; am about to → was about to.
The point of reference is a past moment; the action is in the future compared with that moment. It may or may not have happened: the context tells you.

lignes: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
We were leaving the next day, so we packed.
The train was about to leave.
The meeting was due to start at nine.
He was to become president ten years later.

sections.titre: Was / were going to: past intention or prediction
texte: “Was going to” expresses an intention you had in the past. Very often it did not happen, and we add “but…”: “I was going to call you, but I forgot.”
It also expresses a prediction based on evidence in the past: “The sky was black. It was obviously going to rain.”
In speech, “was going to” often sounds like “was gonna”; only write it like that in very informal messages.
exemples: I was going to buy a new phone, but the price went up.
A plan that changed.
We were going to visit Kribi, but it rained all week.
A plan that didn't happen.
I could see she was going to cry.
A prediction from evidence.
Sorry, I wasn't going to say anything, but…
I didn't intend to speak.

sections.titre: Would: the future seen from the past
texte: “Would” is “will” moved into the past. It appears in reported speech (“She said she would call”) and in stories, to announce what was going to happen: “In 1995, she met the man she would marry two years later.”
Careful: you cannot use “would” for a personal intention that didn't happen. “I would call you yesterday” is wrong; say “I was going to call you yesterday”.
exemples: I knew she would win.
Future from a past point of view.
He promised he would help us the next day.
Reported promise.
Nobody thought the project would succeed.
A past opinion about the future.
Little by little, the village would become a town.
Narrative: what was going to happen.

sections.titre: Was about to, was + -ing, was due to
texte: “Was about to + base form”: an action that was going to happen immediately. We often add “when” for an interruption: “We were about to leave when the phone rang.” Add “just” for emphasis: “I was just about to call you!”
“Was + -ing”: an arrangement planned in the past, like the present continuous for the future: “I was flying to Montreal the next morning, so I went to bed early.”
“Was due to + base form”: an official time or scheduled event: “The flight was due to land at 6, but it was delayed.”
exemples: The film was about to start when she arrived.
Immediate future in the past.
I was just about to call you!
Common phrase.
She was meeting her parents that evening, so she couldn't stay.
A past arrangement.
The new bridge was due to open in May.
A scheduled event.

sections.titre: Was to: destiny and formal arrangements
texte: “Was / were to + base form” is more literary. It announces something that really happened later (destiny): “He was to become one of the greatest writers of his generation.”
“Was to have + past participle” means that the planned arrangement did not happen: “The wedding was to have taken place in June.” This form is formal and rare in speech.
“Was supposed to” is the everyday equivalent for a plan or duty that was not carried out: “We were supposed to meet at eight, but he never came.”
exemples: Nelson Mandela was to spend 27 years in prison.
A historical fact, seen from an earlier point.
The concert was to have taken place in Liège.
It was planned, but it didn't happen.
We were supposed to meet at eight.
Everyday English.

texte: As with “will”, do not use “would” after when, as soon as, before, after or until. Use the past simple: “He said he would phone when he arrived” (not “when he would arrive”).
In a past narrative, don't switch to the present: “I thought it is going to rain” is wrong; say “I thought it was going to rain”.
After “going to” and “about to”, always use the base form: “I was going to go”, not “I was going to went”.
exemples: She told me she would call as soon as she got home.
“got”, not “would get”.
I thought it was going to rain, so I took an umbrella.
Keep the past.

formule: was / were going to · would · was / were + -ing · was / were about to · was / were due to · was / were to + base form
prononciation: “was going to” is often reduced to /wəz ˈɡʌnə/ (“was gonna”) in fast speech.
“would” contracts to 'd: “I knew she'd win” /aɪ njuː ʃiːd ˈwɪn/.
“were about to”: /wər əˈbaʊt tə/, with a linking r in British English.
In “I was going to call you, but…”, the voice rises on “call” and then falls: the intonation tells the listener the plan didn't happen.
“due” is /djuː/ in British English and /duː/ in American English.
erreurs: I knew she will be late.
I knew she would be late.
Future seen from the past: would.
I would call you yesterday, but I forgot.
I was going to call you yesterday, but I forgot.
Past intention that didn't happen: was going to.
He said he would phone when he would arrive.
He said he would phone when he arrived.
No “would” after when.
We were about leaving when it started to rain.
We were about to leave when it started to rain.
be about to + base form.
She was to became famous.
She was to become famous.
was to + base form.
I thought it is going to rain.
I thought it was going to rain.
Past narrative: was going to.
I was going to went to the gym.
I was going to go to the gym.
going to + base form.

dialogue.contexte: In Nairobi, Wanjiru and her Belgian colleague Thomas are back at the office after a long weekend.
lignes: So, did you go to the Maasai Mara in the end?
No! We were going to leave on Friday morning, but the car broke down.
Oh no. I knew that old car would cause problems one day.
would: future seen from the past.
We were just about to get on the road when the engine started smoking.
He promised he would fix it by Saturday, but he didn't have the part.
Too bad. Our flight to Mombasa was due to leave on Sunday, so we had the same stress!
Well, I was going to call you to ask for a lift, but I didn't want to ruin your weekend.

mots: I intended to call you, but I forgot.
We originally planned to leave on Friday.
in the end, after a long time
The trip turned out to be a disaster.
to happen or be in a way you didn't expect
There was a last-minute change of plan.
happening just before it is too late
expected to happen or arrive at a certain time
a power that seems to decide what happens
I didn't expect him to come.
to say that you will certainly do something; a statement like this
Can you give me a lift to the airport?
a free ride in someone's car (US: ride)

exercices.consigne: Explain the meaning of each sentence.
items: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
A past intention that didn't happen.
She knew she would never see him again.
Future seen from the past (and it happened).
We were leaving the next morning, so we packed our bags.
An arrangement planned in the past.
The train was about to leave when I arrived.
Immediate future in the past.

exercices.consigne: Complete with the right form (was going to, would, was about to, was due to).
items: I ___ (go) to the gym yesterday, but it was closed.
was going to go
When I met Paul in 2015, I didn't know he ___ (become) my husband.
would become
We ___ (just / leave) when the phone rang. (immediately)
were just about to leave
He promised he ___ (help) us the next day.
would help
The meeting ___ (start) at nine, but it began at ten. (scheduled)
was due to start
Look at those clouds! I knew it ___ (rain).
was going to rain (or would rain)

exercices.consigne: Rewrite each sentence with the form given.
items: I planned to visit my aunt, but I didn't have time. (was going to)
I was going to visit my aunt, but I didn't have time.
She said: “I will send the report tomorrow.” (reported speech)
She said (that) she would send the report the next day.
We had arranged to meet at eight. (was / were + -ing)
We were meeting at eight.
The plane was going to take off in a few seconds. (about to)
The plane was about to take off.
Later he became a famous writer. (was to)
He was (later) to become a famous writer.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I knew she will be late.
I knew she would be late.
I would call you yesterday, but I forgot.
I was going to call you yesterday, but I forgot.
He said he would phone when he would arrive.
He said he would phone when he arrived.
We were about leaving when it started to rain.
We were about to leave when it started to rain.
I ___ call you, but I forgot. (was going to / would)
was going to
She knew she ___ never forget that day. (would / was about to)
would
We ___ leave when she arrived. (were about to / would)
were about to
He didn't know yet that he ___ become president. (was to / was about to)
was to (or would)

exercices.consigne: Tell the story of a plan that didn't go as expected (4–5 sentences), with at least four future-in-the-past forms.
items: Example answer

Last summer, I was going to spend two weeks in Canada with my cousin. My flight was due to leave Brussels on 2 July. I was just about to go to the airport when I realised my passport had expired. I had promised my cousin I would arrive on time, so I felt terrible. In the end, I flew a week later, and it turned out to be the best holiday of my life.

a_retenir: Future in the past = move the auxiliary back: will → would, am going to → was going to, am about to → was about to.
was going to = a past intention, often not carried out. Never “I would call you yesterday”.
would = future seen from the past in stories and reported speech (I knew he would come).
was about to (immediate), was + -ing (arrangement), was due to (schedule), was to (destiny, formal).
No “would” after when / as soon as: “when he arrived”.
